The Washington Commanders' rushing attack will be without Jacory Croskey-Merritt for their Monday Night Football showdown against the San Francisco 49ers. He's dealing with a groin injury, and head coach Dan Quinn had no choice but to rule him out after he missed practice all week.

Though disappointing, especially considering Croskey-Merritt is coming off his most productive game of the season, others have to step up. This means more is required of free-agent signing Rachaad White, who's not quite met expectations so far.

White was an intriguing addition to the Commanders' ranks in free agency. He bet on himself with a one-year, $2 million deal , and his previous connection to quarterback Jayden Daniels from their time at Arizona State added another layer of intrigue.

After a week of intense criticism and ridicule, the Washington Commanders are no doubt looking forward to getting back on the field and righting the wrong from their overtime calamity against the New York Giants .

Unfortunately for head coach Dan Quinn's squad, the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers are waiting for them on Monday Night Football .

The Niners have been in sensational form to begin the campaign. They are 5-0, despite missing some top stars to injury. Head coach Kyle Shanahan is finding ways to win, and they have already beaten the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos this season to cement their status as a real contender.

This will be a difficult proposition for Washington to overcome. At the same time, nobody is expecting anything other than a heavy defeat, which could work in their favor.

They can play with more freedom. They can relax, though there is pressure to put up a fight, at the very least. And after completely botching their chance to win in Week 5 , fans will be watching their response closely.

This is no time for half-measures. Everyone must come together, and the Commanders must put in maximum effort before the bye week. And when expectations are low, that's when this squad tends to do well.

Hopefully, that will be the case at Levi's Stadium. But these seven Commanders must deliver with the prime-time spotlight shining on them

The Commanders are moving on from a frustrating overtime tie to the New York Giants as they prepare to face the undefeated San Francisco 49ers on Monday night.

The Commanders have little time to dwell on last week's mistakes with a trip to Santa Clara, California, next on the schedule. But players say the loss offered important lessons, particularly about executing in critical moments.

"You could be prepared for a moment, but unless you execute, it doesn't really mean much," wide receiver Terry McLaurin said. "What I think showed up is we didn't execute it."

McLaurin compared the experience to studying for a test but freezing when it is time to answer the questions.

The Commanders now face a significant challenge against a San Francisco team that has yet to lose this season. Washington's defense is preparing for an offense that averages 365 total yards per game and features several key playmakers, including quarterback Brock Purdy, running back Christian McCaffrey, wide receiver Mike Evans and tight end George Kittle.

Defenders emphasized the importance of staying disciplined and recognizing offensive formations, particularly with San Francisco's use of motion and players who can make plays in different situations.

Knowing where the 49ers' primary targets line up will be critical, while maintaining consistency will be just as important when things go wrong.

"When good things happen, you keep charging them. When bad things happen, keep charging them," defensive back Amik Robertson said. "That's just the nature of the game."

Washington's offense also faces a challenge against San Francisco's defense, with linebacker Fred Warner among the players the Commanders must account for.

Receivers stressed the importance of protecting the football while navigating traffic and staying out of third-and-long situations, when the 49ers' defense can take advantage of predictable passing downs.

Monday's game also begins a stretch of primetime appearances for Washington. Four of the Commanders' next five games will be played in front of a national audience.

McLaurin said he enjoys the opportunity to showcase the team on a national stage.

For the Commanders, the immediate focus is on applying the lessons from last week's tie and executing against one of the league's toughest opponents.

The Washington Commanders went 12-5 in the first season under head coach Dan Quinn in 2024. Since then, ahead of Week 6 of the 2026 NFL regular season, his team has posted a 6-15-1 record, putting his job security in serious jeopardy in Year 3.

Beyond the lack of success in the past two seasons, the Commanders' botching of a potential overtime victory over the Giants in Week 5 has made his seat hotter. Quinn will need Washington to show improved results soon to extend his term to four years.

Should owner Josh Harris want to make another change and hire the 32nd head coach in franchise history, here would be his options, starting with one in-house.

Commanders' 7 best coaching candidates for 2027

1. David Blough, Commanders offensive coordinator (age: 31)

Would the Commanders follow the Bills ' example and remove an older defensive-minded coach in Quinn (56) and promote his offensive coordinator? Don't rule it out, despite Blough, a former journeyman backup, being so young.

Bold offensive-minded hires have worked well for several teams. It's a good bet Washington pivots from old-school defense to new-school offense with its new leader. Blough should get a chance because of good early work getting Jayden Daniels back on track.

By the middle of the fourth quarter on Sunday, that reality finally reached the fans by the show of large sections of empty seats at Lincoln Financial Field.

Get ready for a lot of that in the coming months, because the rest of the Eagles' 2026 season will be devoted to evaluating who to keep and who to discard after the Eagles fell to the Carolina Panthers, 25-14, at the Linc.

The Eagles are now 2-4— and through , regardless of how bad the NFC East looks.

It was the Eagles' fourth-straight loss, making it the first time they have lost four-straight games since Doug Peterson's 4-11-1 season in 2020—and the first four-game losing streak in Nick Sirianni's tenure.

Going to the Linc are still great ways to fill autumn Sunday afternoons, sans winning.

But after the greatest four-year stretch in Eagles' history, with the mounting cracks in the wall the Eagles were bound to collapse.

The Eagles may be expecting Tanner McKee to be the next coming of Nick Foles (or Tom Brady, according to Zack Baun). The problem is this fanbase knows Nick Foles. It watched Nick Foles win a Super Bowl.

New York Giants fans overwhelmingly believe J.J. McCarthy should be the team's quarterback beginning this Sunday against the Houston Texans.

Eighty-one percent of the 751 voters in our poll think McCarthy should replace Jameis Winston as the starter when the Giants face the Houston Texans this Sunday.

Head coach John Harbaugh wasn't ready to make that decision in his post-game press conference.

"I can't answer that now," Harbaugh said. "The game just ended ten minutes ago.

"It's not even up for discussion or conversation right now. We've got to go back and go to work. I have no problem with Jameis whatsoever. I love the way he competes, I love the way he fights, all those kind of things. He was up and down today for sure, but those things will all be decided not ten minutes after a game."

It is, though, a decision Harbaugh has to make.

When the Giants acquired McCarthy from the Minnesota Vikings a few weeks ago for a fifth-round pick, it seemed clear Harbaugh would face this decision at some point. I'm sure he knew that, too. I doubt, though, that anyone expected that choice to have to come now.

Harbaugh put McCarthy into Sunday's game with the Giants trailing by 24 points and 11:25 remaining. Most likely, he figured that in what seemed like a lost cause, it was a good chance to give McCarthy some snaps running the offense.

McCarthy's first series ended in an interception on a ball nowhere near intended receiver Malachi Fields.

C.J. Donaldson of New Orleans fumbled. Arvell Reese recovered. McCarthy suddenly started slinging the ball all over the place, throwing for 243 yards in less than a quarter of action. The Giants started scoring, and somehow found themselves with a chance to win the game with :12 left.

The Dallas Cowboys arrived at Lambeau Field needing a response after an ugly loss to Tampa Bay, but another slow offensive performance and unprepared defense left Dallas chasing the game all evening.

Dallas went into halftime down 17-0, with turnovers and penalties repeatedly wasting opportunities leading to Dallas falling to Green Bay 23-13. Here are this week's winners and losers from the game.

Dallas has waited a long time for an interception, and Dee Winters finally delivered one.

Winters read Jordan Love perfectly late in the first quarter, stepped in front of the pass and appeared to return it for a touchdown before replay ruled him down at the Green Bay 42-yard line. Even without the score, it was exactly the type of momentum-changing defensive play Dallas has desperately needed.

The frustrating part was that the offense immediately wasted the opportunity with an interception of its own. That shouldn't take anything away from Winters. On a defense that was searching for takeaways and impact plays, Winters provided one.

The Cowboys needed considerably more from their defensive front after weeks of inconsistent pressure, and Quinnen Williams made his presence felt early.

Williams got to Jordan Love for a sack and helped Dallas produce a much more disruptive start up front. Green Bay found success through the air, but its conventional rushing attack has been much less effective. Williams' sack was one of the Cowboys' biggest early defensive plays and it was needed to try an inject some optimism in a defense that's struggled this season.

This is the type of performance Dallas expected when it paid the price to bring Williams into the middle of the defense. The Cowboys need him affecting games rather than simply occupying blockers, the sack showed exactly that.

For San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy and linebacker Fred Warner , training camp has become an annual battleground. It isn't just about offense versus defense; it's how they can, individually, win the day against each other.

For Purdy specifically, those chess matches are vital because the middle of the field is fertile but dangerous ground in coach Kyle Shanahan's offense. It requires Purdy to layer the ball to his pass catchers between multiple defenders, the type of precision best achieved through repetition against the best middle linebacker in the game. And he has gotten good enough at it that he can even leave Warner grasping at air.

Early in the 49ers' 16th training camp practice this August, he completed a pass over Warner's outstretched arms to wideout Mike Evans for a big gain. But later, Warner broke up similar over-the-middle attempts to wide receiver Demarcus Robinson and running back Kaelon Black . Warner turned and boisterously let Purdy hear about it after both.

As the practice neared its end, Purdy dropped back and saw Warner sink into coverage. Purdy fired it just past Warner's fingertips and into Deebo Samuel Sr .'s waiting hands. Then, Purdy let it fly toward Warner again — verbally. A loud "F— you, Fred" echoed across the field. Moments later, Warner and Purdy stood behind the huddle laughing, and they later acknowledged how such intense practice moments push the other to be better.

articles.title: Inside the Huddle: The NFL's Los Angeles Rams dream team lose again - what is wrong with Sean McVay's side?
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Rams lost for the fourth time this season as they suffered an upset defeat to the Arizona Cardinals in Week Six, leaving them playing catch up in the NFL playoff race; watch the New Orleans Saints take on the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris, live on Sky Sports this Sunday
articles.body:
Sky Sports NFL 's Neil Reynolds and Jeff Reinebold discuss where it is going wrong for Sean McVay's side on the latest episode of Inside the Huddle, after the Rams suffered a shock 18-16 defeat to the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday.

Their latest setback leaves them 2-4 at the bottom of the NFC West, McVay insisting little will change unless his team find a way to stop "beating ourselves".

"Cast your mind back to the summer. It was a dream team," said Reynolds on Inside the Huddle. "There's no such thing as a dream team in the NFL.

"I know we've had them over the years and they've never panned out. It was a dream team. They were the strongest of Super Bowl favourites.

"The Rams didn't just lose this game. They looked really out of sorts, like there was a hangover from the one they might have had against Buffalo on Monday night."

The Rams made the biggest splash of the offseason this year when they traded for Defensive Player of the Year pass rusher Myles Garrett, who remains sidelined since Week One due to injury. They meanwhile lured Aaron Donald out of retirement to bolster a star-studded team already led by MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford, who took the Rams to the NFC Championship Game last season as they were narrowly-beaten by the eventual champion Seattle Seahawks.

For all their talent, the Rams have seen special teams prove a debilitating factor in recent games, and this week cut kicker Harrison Mevis after his poor start to the year. They replaced him with former New Orleans Saints kicker Blake Grupe, who was hurt on Sunday while trying to tackle Devin Duvernay on a return.

The Rams rank last in special teams EPA through six weeks, their struggles haunting them again Sunday when injury to Grupe forced them to go for two points after their first touchdown, which they failed to convert. Punter Ethan Evans later had to attempt the extra point, with backup quarterback Stetson Bennett coming in as the holder.

"The fact you fire your kicker after the Buffalo game, bring in a new guy, and then he gets hurt because you can't cover a kickoff, right? He's trying to make a tackle on a kickoff, he gets hurt, and now your punter is your kicker," said Reinebold.

"They're still very good. And Matthew Stafford throws two touchdowns and no picks and all that, but everything that can go wrong is going wrong.

"Now you can say that the Rams are way better, their roster's way better than the Cardinals, and that's an argument you can make, but these are pro athletes. These are the best there are in the world. And if you give them a chance and you let them hang around, they're good enough to beat you. And that's what happened to the Rams."

Speaking after the game, McVay shouldered the blame while insisting he needed to do a "much better job", saying there were no positives to take from Sunday.

McVay himself has endured a turbulent start to the season, criticising his own decision to fly into Melbourne, Australia just a day before the Rams' defeat to the San Francisco 49ers, before leaving a press conference early and then expressing his anger following the Week Five loss to the Bills.

"Sean McVay's been quite regretful in recent games that he hasn't been aggressive enough or his play calling hasn't been on point," said Reynolds.

"Every bounce seems to be going against them at the moment, but they just look out of sync. Sean McVay is intense. He is a hundred miles an hour. He openly admitted, he told me this the summer after losing to the Patriots in the Super Bowl that he overprepared because it was Bill Belichick.

"He ran his team too much mentally going into that game, put too much on their plates. He's got to balance that, hasn't he now? To not hit the panic button and to just try and methodically work your way out of this."

The Rams visit the Las Vegas Raiders in Week Seven, before facing Justin Herbert's limping Los Angeles Chargers.
